classification.difficultyReason: Use the calculated IQR to construct an upper outlier boundary and justify a comparison; also plot the supplied regression equation and recognise prediction beyond the observed range as extrapolation.

content.prompt: The scatterplot shows the relationship between expenditure per primary school student, as a percentage of a country’s Gross Domestic Product (GDP), and the life expectancy in years for 15 countries.

spec.description: Rectangular scatterplot with 15 distinct diamond markers, major solid grid lines, dotted minor subdivisions, axis ticks, titles and arrow-end coordinate cues. Marker locations are read approximately from the printed graph; no exact dataset is asserted. Source grey marker fills are replaced by black outlines with white interiors.
spec.mathematics: Horizontal range 0–30, labelled every 5, minor subdivisions every 1. Vertical range 0–90, labelled every 10, minor subdivisions every 2. Two vertically adjacent points near x=11 remain distinct.
spec.answerVisibility: Supplied points and grid are permanent givens. The regression line is absent from the student graph.

children.label: a
children.prompt: For the given data, the correlation coefficient, $r$, is 0.83. What does this indicate about the relationship between expenditure per primary school student and life expectancy for the 15 countries?

answer.short: There is a strong positive correlation between expenditure per primary school student and life expectancy.
answer.worked: Since $r=0.83$, there is a strong positive correlation: countries with greater expenditure per primary school student tend to have higher life expectancy.

children.label: b
children.prompt: For the data representing expenditure per primary school student, $Q_L=8.4$ and $Q_U=22.5$. Calculate the interquartile range.

answer.worked:
$$\begin{align*}\mathrm{IQR}&=Q_U-Q_L\\&=22.5-8.4\\&=14.1\end{align*}$$
The interquartile range is 14.1 percentage points.

children.label: c
children.prompt: Another country has an expenditure per primary school student of 47.6% of its GDP. Would this country be an outlier for this set of data? Justify your answer with calculations.

answer.short: Yes. The upper outlier boundary is $22.5+1.5(14.1)=43.65\%$, and $47.6\%>43.65\%$.
answer.worked:
$$\begin{align*}\text{Upper boundary}&=Q_U+1.5\,\mathrm{IQR}\\&=22.5+1.5(14.1)\\&=43.65\end{align*}$$
Since $47.6>43.65$, this country would be an outlier for expenditure per primary school student.

children.label: d
children.prompt:
On the scatterplot, draw the least-squares line of best fit $y=1.29x+49.9$.

Using this line, estimate the life expectancy in a country which has an expenditure per primary school student of 18% of its GDP. Give your answer to the nearest whole year.

answer.short: See the plotted line. About 73 years.
answer.worked:
Draw the straight line through $(0,49.9)$ and $(30,88.6)$.

$$\begin{align*}y&=1.29(18)+49.9\\&=73.12\end{align*}$$
The estimated life expectancy is about 73 years.

spec.sourceRegion: Shared scatterplot and fourth response prompt
spec.description: Equation-derived regression-line overlay using exactly the base graph coordinate units and bounding box.
spec.mathematics: Plot y=1.29x+49.9 for 0≤x≤30. Endpoints are (0,49.9) and (30,88.6).

children.label: e
children.prompt: Why is this line NOT useful for predicting life expectancy in a country which has expenditure per primary school student of 60% of its GDP?

answer.short: 60% is far outside the observed expenditure range, so this would be unreliable extrapolation.
answer.worked: An expenditure of 60% is far outside the observed data range. Using the line would involve extrapolation, and the observed relationship may not continue that far.
